lessons.title: The flower and pollination
lessons.programRef: GCE O Level Biology — Flower structure, pollination, fertilisation, seeds, vegetative propagation (to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Name the parts of a flower and their functions.
Define pollination and compare insect- and wind-pollinated flowers.
Describe fertilisation in a flowering plant.
reviewNotes: Petal count/shape is not typical of any single species.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Parts of a flower
blocks.md:
- **Sepals**: protect the bud. **Petals**: attract insects (in insect-pollinated flowers).
- **Stamen** (male): **anther** makes **pollen grains** (male gametes inside); **filament** holds it up.
- **Carpel** (female): **stigma** receives pollen; **style** joins stigma to **ovary**; the ovary contains **ovules** (each holds an egg cell).

blocks.caption: Longitudinal section of a flower (schematic).
blocks.alt: A flower with two pink petals, a green ovary with two ovules, a style topped by a yellow stigma and two stamens, each with an anther on a filament; leader lines label each part.

blocks.title: Pollination
blocks.md:
**Pollination** is the transfer of pollen from an **anther** to a **stigma** of a flower of the same species. **Self-pollination**: on the same plant. **Cross-pollination**: to a different plant of the same species; this gives more variation.

Agents of pollination are insects (bees) and wind.

blocks.title: Insect- and wind-pollinated flowers
blocks.md:
- **Insect-pollinated**: large, brightly coloured petals, scent and **nectar**; small amounts of sticky or spiny pollen; stigma sticky and inside the flower.
- **Wind-pollinated** (maize, grasses): small, dull flowers without nectar or scent; anthers hang outside; huge amounts of **light, smooth pollen**; **feathery** stigmas outside to catch pollen.

blocks.title: Fertilisation
blocks.md:
A pollen grain lands on a compatible stigma and grows a **pollen tube** down the style to the ovary and into an ovule. The **male nucleus** fuses with the **egg nucleus** in the ovule: this is **fertilisation** and it forms a **zygote**.

After fertilisation the **ovule becomes the seed** and the **ovary becomes the fruit**; the petals and other parts wither.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Pollination is *not* fertilisation: pollination is transfer of pollen; fertilisation is the fusion of nuclei.
- Pollen is made in the *anther*, not the filament.
- Wind-pollinated flowers do not need bright petals.

blocks.title: Which kind of flower?
blocks.statement: A flower has small green petals, long stamens hanging out of the flower and feathery stigmas. How is it pollinated and why?
steps: Small dull petals give no attraction for insects.
Hanging anthers release pollen easily to the wind, and feathery stigmas trap airborne pollen.

blocks.title: From flower to fruit
blocks.statement: In a pawpaw flower fertilisation has taken place. State what the ovule and ovary become.
steps: After fertilisation the ovule develops into the seed.
The ovary wall develops into the fruit.
blocks.answer: Ovule to seed; ovary to fruit.

objectives: State the conditions needed for germination and design an experiment.
Describe asexual reproduction (vegetative propagation) and compare it with sexual reproduction.
reviewNotes: Germination bar-chart values are invented teaching data.
Plant examples (cassava, plantain, yam) are common in Cameroon; check which the syllabus prefers.

blocks.title: Seed dispersal
blocks.md: **Dispersal** carries seeds away from the parent plant, which reduces competition for light, water and minerals and spreads the species. Methods: **wind** (winged or feathery seeds); **animals** (hooked fruits stick to fur; fleshy fruits are eaten and seeds pass out in faeces); **water** (coconut); **explosive** (pods dry and split open, throwing seeds away).

blocks.title: Conditions for germination
blocks.md: Seeds need **water** (to activate enzymes), **oxygen** (for respiration), and a suitable **temperature** (warm). Light is *not* needed for most seeds. Stored food in the cotyledons or endosperm feeds the embryo until the leaves can photosynthesise.

blocks.caption: An experiment on germination (teaching data).
blocks.alt: A bar chart: 18 seeds out of 20 germinate with water, air and warmth; 0 with no water; 1 without air; 2 in the cold.

blocks.title: Vegetative propagation
blocks.md:
**Asexual reproduction** produces new plants from **one parent** without gametes; the offspring are genetically identical (**clones**). Examples: **cassava stem cuttings**, **banana and plantain suckers**, **yam setts** (pieces of tuber), sugar-cane cuttings.

Advantages: fast, keeps good qualities, no pollination needed. Disadvantage: no variation, so a disease can affect the whole crop.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Germination needs *oxygen*; seeds under water-logged soil may rot.
- Light and soil are *not* necessary for germination.
- Clones are identical; sexual reproduction gives variation.

blocks.title: Experiment design
blocks.statement: Design a fair test to show that seeds need water to germinate.
steps: Set up two dishes with 20 identical bean seeds each: one with damp cotton wool (test) and one with dry cotton wool (control).
Keep temperature, air supply and time the same, so water is the only difference; count germinated seeds after a few days.
blocks.answer: Only water is changed; the damp dish germinates and the dry dish does not.

blocks.title: Percent germinated
blocks.statement: In a farm in Mbouda, 18 of 20 bean seeds germinate in the warm damp dish and 2 of 20 in a cold dish. Calculate percentage germination in each.
